cards.back: Contiguous memory, fixed or dynamic size. Access O(1), search O(n), insert/delete at end O(1) amortized, at middle O(n).
Nodes with data + pointer to next. Insert/delete at head O(1), search O(n), no random access. Singly or doubly linked.
LIFO (Last In, First Out). Push/pop O(1). Use cases: undo, call stack, parenthesis matching, DFS.
FIFO (First In, First Out). Enqueue/dequeue O(1). Use cases: BFS, task scheduling, buffering.
Key-value pairs. Average O(1) insert, delete, lookup. Worst case O(n) with collisions. Uses hash function.
Each node has at most 2 children. Left < parent < right. Average O(log n) operations. Degrades to O(n) if unbalanced.
Self-balancing BST. Height difference between subtrees ≤ 1. Guarantees O(log n) operations via rotations.
Self-balancing BST with colored nodes. Less strictly balanced than AVL but fewer rotations on insert/delete. O(log n) operations.
Complete binary tree. Min-heap: parent ≤ children. Insert O(log n), extract-min O(log n), peek O(1). Used in priority queues.
Tree for storing strings. Each node = character. O(m) search/insert where m = key length. Used for autocomplete, spell check.
Vertices + edges. Directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Represented as adjacency list or adjacency matrix.
List: O(V+E) space, efficient for sparse graphs. Matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup, better for dense graphs.
Search sorted array by halving. O(log n) time, O(1) space. Compare target with middle, go left or right.
Repeatedly swap adjacent elements if out of order. O(n²) average/worst. O(1) space. Stable. Simple but slow.
Find minimum, place at front, repeat. O(n²) always. O(1) space. Not stable. Minimal swaps (n-1).
Build sorted array one element at a time. O(n²) average, O(n) best (nearly sorted). Stable. Good for small/nearly sorted data.
Divide array in half, sort each, merge. O(n log n) always. O(n) space. Stable. Good for linked lists and external sorting.
Pick pivot, partition around it, recurse. O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst. O(log n) space. Not stable. Fast in practice.
Build max-heap, extract max repeatedly. O(n log n) always. O(1) space. Not stable. In-place but poor cache performance.
Count occurrences of each value. O(n + k) where k = range. O(k) space. Stable. Only for integers in known range.
Explore graph level by level using a queue. O(V+E). Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs. Use for level-order traversal.
Explore graph as deep as possible using a stack/recursion. O(V+E). Use for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.
Shortest path from source to all vertices in weighted graph (non-negative weights). O((V+E) log V) with min-heap.
Solve problems by breaking into overlapping subproblems. Store results (memoization/tabulation). Examples: Fibonacci, knapsack, LCS.
Make locally optimal choice at each step. Doesn't always find global optimum. Examples: Dijkstra's, Huffman coding, activity selection.
Split problem into subproblems, solve recursively, combine results. Examples: merge sort, quick sort, binary search.
Describes upper bound of time/space complexity. Common: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ), O(n!).

cards.front: Time Complexity: O(1) vs O(n) vs O(log n)
cards.back: O(1): constant, independent of input size. O(n): linear, scales with input. O(log n): logarithmic, halves each step (binary search).
Average cost per operation over a sequence. Example: dynamic array doubling — individual insert may be O(n), but amortized O(1).
Function calls itself with a smaller input. Needs base case and recursive case. Uses call stack. Can be replaced with iteration.
Use two indices to traverse array. Approaches: start+end (sorted arrays), slow+fast (linked lists). Often reduces O(n²) to O(n).
Maintain a window of elements and slide it across data. O(n) for problems like max sum subarray, longest substring without repeats.
Linear ordering of directed acyclic graph (DAG) vertices. Each edge u→v means u comes before v. Uses DFS or Kahn's algorithm (BFS). O(V+E).
Tracks elements in disjoint sets. Operations: find (which set?), union (merge sets). With path compression + rank: near O(1) per operation.
Memoization: top-down DP, cache recursive results. Tabulation: bottom-up DP, fill table iteratively. Same results, different approaches.
